summary: The bill restores a first-to-invent U.S. patent system by repealing key parts of the 2011 America Invents Act, eliminates inter partes and post-grant reviews along with the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, bars automatic publication of applications, and strengthens patents as private property that courts alone can invalidate.

scores.thoughts: Section 6 creates a revolving fund for USPTO fees, makes them available without fiscal year limitation or diversion to other uses, and terminates the prior reserve fund. This is a structural change to how patent office operations are funded from user fees rather than general appropriations. It does not expand or reduce overall government spending levels; it merely insulates existing fee revenue from congressional redirection. The bill therefore has only tangential, minor implications for government spending.
The bill contains no provisions altering tax rates, tax credits, deductions, or any revenue-raising measures. All changes are confined to patent law and USPTO administration.

While stronger patent rights can indirectly affect pharmaceutical pricing and innovation, the bill makes no targeted changes to healthcare delivery, insurance, drug pricing, or public coverage programs. Any link is too attenuated to register.
No provisions address firearms, background checks, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address visas, border security, asylum, or immigration enforcement.
No provisions address reproductive rights, funding for abortion services, or related regulations.
No provisions address defense budgets, procurement, or military R&D.
No provisions address environmental regulations, emissions standards, or conservation programs.
No provisions address welfare programs, food assistance, housing subsidies, or entitlement spending.
No provisions address schools, student aid, school choice, or federal education policy.
No provisions address controlled substances, decriminalization, or enforcement priorities.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal procedure outside the narrow context of patent validity challenges.

The bill restores a first-to-invent system and strengthens domestic patent rights, which can indirectly influence U.S. innovation competitiveness, but it contains no tariff, trade-agreement, or import/export measures. The connection is too indirect.
The USPTO funding changes are revenue-neutral to the Treasury because they rely on existing user fees. No deficit or debt-reduction measures are included.
No provisions address nondiscrimination protections, marriage, or LGBTQ-specific legal rights.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international development, or aid programs.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or campaign finance.

Section 7 restores patent eligibility for software inventions, which affects the tech sector, but the bill does not regulate data collection, surveillance, platform liability, or privacy standards. The link is incidental.
No provisions address collective bargaining, worker protections, or union governance.
No provisions address religious exemptions, conscience protections, or conflicts between civil rights and religious liberty.
